sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Foundation design for buildings is typically performed in accordance with the current version of the Uniform Building Code (UBC) or the International Building Code (IBC). These codes provide minimum criteria for design of building foundations, including considerations for frost protection; maximum presumptive bearing stresses; and dead, live, wind, seismic and other loads.
key_points: Building foundation design governed by UBC or IBC codes
Codes provide minimum criteria for frost protection, presumptive bearing stresses, and load combinations
Design must address dead, live, wind, seismic, and other load types
Code requirements represent minimum standards; site-specific analysis may exceed them
sections.applicability: General introduction to building foundation design and governing codes.

sections.title: Geotechnical Investigation
sections.body: The field and laboratory procedures for geotechnical investigation of a building site are the same as described in Chapter 4. The extent of sampling and testing should be commensurate with the performance expectation and importance of the structure. A maintenance facility, for instance, may include several one- and two-story structures, including an equipment bay, that are constructed as slabs-on-grade with spread footing support of lightweight column and wall loads. The subsurface investigation for this type of facility should be sufficient to describe the vertical and lateral extent and variability of foundation bearing soils beneath the structures. A 1,500 to 2,000 m^2 facility will typically require a minimum of three to five borings or test pits that extend at least 3 to 9 m (10 to 30 ft). The required quantity of subsurface information will depend on the geotechnical engineer's confidence that the subsurface conditions are adequately defined to proceed with confidence in designing a shallow foundation system.
key_points: Investigation procedures follow Chapter 4 guidance
Sampling and testing extent should match structure importance and performance expectations
A 1,500-2,000 m^2 facility typically requires 3-5 borings or test pits
Borings should extend at least 3 to 9 m (10 to 30 ft) depth
Investigation must describe vertical and lateral extent of bearing soils
Engineer must have confidence that subsurface conditions are adequately defined
sections.applicability: Planning subsurface investigations for building foundation projects.

sections.title: Shallow Foundation Types
sections.body: The types of shallow foundations used to support buildings are similar to those described in Chapter 2, with the notable difference being generally much smaller dimensions.
key_points: Building shallow foundations are similar to transportation foundations but generally smaller
Three main types: isolated spread footings, continuous strip footings, and mat foundations
sections.applicability: Overview of shallow foundation types for buildings.

sections.title: Isolated Spread Footings
sections.body: Isolated spread footings are frequently used to support individual or occasionally multiple column loads for buildings. Depending on the anticipated potential for differential movements or the potential for high floor loads, the footings may or may not be constructed integral with slabs-on-grade. It may be preferable for slabs to bear on the subgrade soils independently from footings. For lightly loaded structures on compressible soil, it can be economical to partially overexcavate the poor foundation soils and replace them with compacted granular backfill to limit the potential for settlement or bearing capacity problems.
key_points: Used to support individual or multiple column loads in buildings
May or may not be integral with slabs-on-grade depending on differential movement potential
Slabs may bear independently on subgrade soils separate from footings
Overexcavation and replacement with compacted granular backfill is economical for lightly loaded structures on compressible soil
Controls settlement and bearing capacity problems in poor soils
sections.applicability: Design of isolated spread footings for building column and wall loads.

sections.title: Continuous Strip Footings
sections.body: Continuous strip footings are frequently used to support perimeter and load-bearing walls. Where designed and constructed continuous with slabs-on-grade, the footings can be built as thickened edges to achieve the minimum depth requirements for bearing capacity and frost protection.
key_points: Used to support perimeter and load-bearing walls
Can be constructed continuous with slabs-on-grade as thickened edges
Must meet minimum depth requirements for bearing capacity and frost protection
sections.applicability: Design of continuous strip footings for building perimeter and load-bearing walls.

sections.title: Mat Foundations
sections.body: Mats are heavily reinforced concrete foundations that usually cover the entire plan area of a building. Mat foundations may be designed to minimize differential settlements. Mats are usually more economical and preferable when column loads are so large that more than 50 percent of the plan area would be covered by spread footings (Peck et al., 1974). Mats can be used to create deep basements, distribute column loads more uniformly and provide basement slabs (water barrier). Mats may be used when the foundation soil has a low bearing capacity or large differential settlements are anticipated. Mats, by design, are rigid elements that distribute column and wall loads over a larger area, thus reducing the magnitude of the vertical stress on the foundation soil. This not only decreases the stress but also produces a more uniform settlement profile and subsequently reduces differential settlement. The applied stress on the subgrade soil directly below the spread footings is higher than directly below the mat; however, this condition reverses with depth. Additionally, a mat foundation is preferred for a subsurface soil profile containing erratic changes in strength and/or stiffness because the mat tends to bridge over these erratic loose zones better than isolated footings and is expected to undergo smaller differential displacements (about 50 percent less).
key_points: Heavily reinforced concrete foundations covering entire building plan area
Preferred when spread footings would cover more than 50% of plan area
Reduces vertical stress magnitude and produces more uniform settlement profile
Differential displacements approximately 50% less than isolated footings
Can create deep basements and serve as water barriers
Bridges over erratic soil zones with variable strength/stiffness
Applied stress at surface higher under spread footings, but reverses with depth

Figure 8-2: Mat Foundation on a Dense Sand Stratum with Erratic Distribution of Pockets of Loose Sand
sections.applicability: Selection and design of mat foundations for buildings with high loads, poor soils, or erratic subsurface conditions.

sections.title: Allowable Bearing Stresses
sections.body: This section covers settlement and bearing capacity limitations for building foundations.
key_points: Allowable bearing stresses controlled by both settlement and bearing capacity criteria
Settlement limitations often govern for granular soils and wide footings
Bearing capacity limitations may govern for narrow footings on clay
sections.applicability: Determination of allowable bearing stresses for building foundations.

sections.title: Settlement Limitations
sections.body: Tolerable total and differential movements for buildings, like bridges, are strongly a function of the materials and methods used to construct the building. Steel frame buildings are capable of withstanding surprisingly large differential movements without experiencing structural distress or damage. However, such movement may result in objectionable appearances of wall facings and coverings. Masonry structures, on the other hand, are relatively settlement intolerant and may experience structural distress (cracking) if angular distortions exceed 1/300. In practice, bearing stresses are typically limited so that total settlements are on the order of 25 mm (1 in) and differential settlements about half the total settlement. In designing building foundations, considerable benefits can be derived by permanently excavating a portion of the soil by including a basement. This reduces the net increase in stresses on the subgrade, which in turn reduces or eliminates consolidation even in normally consolidated soils.
key_points: Settlement tolerance depends on building materials and construction methods
Steel frame buildings tolerate large differential movements but may show cosmetic damage
Masonry structures experience cracking if angular distortions exceed 1/300
Total settlements typically limited to 25 mm (1 in)
Differential settlements typically limited to about half the total settlement (12.5 mm)
Basement excavation reduces net stress increase and can eliminate consolidation
Compensated foundations (basement excavation) beneficial even in normally consolidated soils
sections.applicability: Establishing settlement criteria for building foundation design.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity Limitations
sections.body: Due to the relatively small width of spread footings for buildings, the potential for bearing capacity failure may control the design of footings, especially foundations on clay. Knowing that most building foundations for lightweight one- and two-story frame construction have widths of about 0.5 to 1.0 m, and referring to Figure 5-1, it can be seen that these values fall to the left, in the bearing capacity limited portion of the chart.
key_points: Bearing capacity failure may control design for small building footings, especially on clay
Typical building footing widths are 0.5 to 1.0 m for lightweight one- and two-story construction
Small footing widths fall in the bearing capacity limited region of design charts (Figure 5-1)
Bearing capacity more critical than settlement for narrow footings on cohesive soils
sections.applicability: Assessing bearing capacity limitations for narrow building footings.

sections.title: Overturning and Eccentricity
sections.body: Spread footings for buildings are designed to maintain a minimum factor of safety against overturning of at least 1.5. Eccentricity may also be checked using the procedures in Chapter 6, although this is generally not part of the code requirements for design of buildings.
key_points: Minimum factor of safety against overturning is 1.5 for building spread footings
Eccentricity can be checked using Chapter 6 procedures
Eccentricity check is generally not required by building codes but is good practice
sections.applicability: Checking overturning stability and eccentricity for building spread footings.

sections.title: Sliding and Passive Resistance
sections.body: The procedures for calculating sliding and passive resistance for building spread footings are described in Chapter 5. A minimum factor of safety of 1.5 should be provided for sliding stability. Due to the generally small width of spread footings used for buildings, inclusion of the passive resistance may be necessary. Because of the differences in strains required to develop sliding and passive resistance, as described in Section 5.4, a practical approach is to include only one-half of the computed passive resistance when combining both sliding and passive components. For narrow footing widths, simply deepening the footing to increase passive resistance may be more practical than attempting construction of a key.
key_points: Minimum factor of safety of 1.5 required for sliding stability
Passive resistance may need to be included due to small footing widths
Use only one-half of computed passive resistance when combining with sliding resistance
Strain incompatibility between sliding and passive resistance requires reduction
Deepening footing is more practical than constructing a shear key for narrow footings
Sliding and passive resistance procedures detailed in Chapter 5 and Section 5.4
sections.applicability: Checking sliding stability of building spread footings.

sections.title: Design of Mat Foundations and Floor Slabs
sections.body: The design of mat foundations should account for bearing capacity, as well as immediate and long-term settlements. The bearing capacity and settlement of a mat foundation may be determined using the methods presented in Chapter 5. Due to the large size of mat foundations, bearing capacity will generally not govern design. Controlling deflections will usually be the most critical aspect of design. Mat settlements can be controlled to some degree with the lower applied soil pressures as compared to isolated or strip spread footings. Also, the volume of soil displaced by the foundation will result in a lower net applied stress that will limit settlement. Mat foundations on cohesive soils (clays) may be controlled by deep-seated bearing capacity. The subsurface explorations must be carried to sufficient depth to assess both deep-seated bearing capacity and the zone of stress influence (Section 5.3) for settlement computation. Due to the large dimensions of a mat, the zone of influence will be deeper than for isolated or strip spread footings. A common design approach for mat foundations uses beam on elastic foundation theory to compute the soil-structure interaction and deflections. The reinforcement of the mat can then be designed based on the deflections computed within the mat. The beam on elastic foundation approach models the support of foundation soils as a bed of discrete elastic springs (Winkler foundation). The soil reaction at any particular point beneath a mat is: q_applied = K_v * y, where q_applied = Applied stress, K_v = Modulus of subgrade reaction (force/length^3), and y = Vertical displacement. The modulus of subgrade reaction can be obtained from Figure 8-3. Note that the notation for the modulus is K_V1 in Figure 8-3. The modulus of subgrade reaction can also be obtained from plate load tests but should be corrected for size and shape effects according to Figure 8-4. The validity of the beam on elastic foundation approach has been called into question due to the fundamental assumption regarding the relative rigidity of the mat as compared to the soil. Also, the modulus of subgrade reaction is not an intrinsic soil property, and is a function not only of the stiffness of the soil, but the stiffness, shape and depth of the mat. Despite these limitations, the method is still a practical and commonly used way of computing displacements to design the structural reinforcement of the mat.
key_points: Mat design must account for bearing capacity, immediate settlement, and long-term settlement
Bearing capacity generally does not govern mat design due to large size
Controlling deflections is typically the most critical design aspect
Deep-seated bearing capacity may control on cohesive soils
Subsurface explorations must reach sufficient depth for deep-seated capacity and settlement zone of influence
Beam on elastic foundation (Winkler) theory is common design approach: q_applied = K_v * y
Modulus of subgrade reaction (K_v) obtained from Figure 8-3 or plate load tests corrected per Figure 8-4
K_v is not an intrinsic soil property; depends on soil stiffness, mat stiffness, shape, and depth
equations: Equation 8-1: q_applied = K_v * y (Winkler foundation model)
figures: Figure 8-4: Analysis of Plate Load Test Results (NAVFAC, 1986a)
sections.applicability: Design of mat foundations and floor slabs for buildings, including Winkler model approach and subgrade reaction determination.
